To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
a model that is a decision model for choice in concurrent chains can account for choice data in concurrent chains.

a decision model for choice in concurrent chains can be derived from an acquisition model that assumes subjects discriminate between short and long delays, and that this model provides a good account of archival data.

a decision model for choice can be derived from a decision model for learning and that it provides a better account of archival choice data than the contextual choice model and the hyperbolic value-addition model.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question, how do subjects choose between two concurrent variable-interval schedules?
understanding the processes that underlie choice and how those processes are influenced by the environment.
a theoretical approach to understanding concurrent choice that has the potential to provide a unified account of both the acquisition and steady-state phases of choice.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the steady-state decision account of choice in concurrent chained schedules provides a superior alternative to the hyperbolic value addition model and the contextual choice model in terms of goodness-of-fit, parsimony, parameter invariance, and the ability to account for choice at the molen level in terms of a model for acquisition.
the decision model is the best model for choice in concurrent chains, but the hyperbolic value added model is the best for choice in simple schedules of reinforcement.
the steady-state decision account provides the most parsimonious and robust account of choice in concurrent-chain schedules.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the decision model provides a parsimonious account of choice in concurrent-chains procedures.
the decision model for choice is the best available model for steady-state responding in concurrent chains.
the decision model provides the most parsimonious account of the data, with the fewest number of free parameters and the most invariant parameters.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the decision model for acquisition can be extended to choice by assuming that subjects choose the alternative that is associated with the higher expected value of the decision model.
a simple decision model can be used as a framework to understand choice behavior in concurrent chains, and it is possible to derive expressions for choice in steady-state conditions.
the decision model for concurrent chains is a viable model for explaining choice in concurrent chains, which can be extended to other choice situations.
